Every discounted cash flow valuation rests on two numbers you made up.
The growth forecast comes from one model, and the discount rate comes
from another. Neither is obliged to agree with the other. The course
teaches the alternative I used to answer one of asset pricing's oldest
questions. You derive both numbers from a single description of the
economy, meaning one consumption process and one set of preferences,
and the same model then prices every claim, from the aggregate stock
market to a portfolio you bring yourself.

The course is built around my paper, *Is the Value Premium a Puzzle?*
Value firms out-earned growth firms by about six percentage points a
year over 1930 to 2003, while their market betas are nearly identical.
Under the CAPM, a higher return requires a higher beta, so the CAPM
cannot price the premium. By the end of the course you will have
rebuilt the general equilibrium model that resolves the puzzle, and you
will have tested it against seventy-four years of data. You will also
have used the model to price a claim of your own.

## The main result

The table below is the result the course builds toward. The model is
calibrated to consumption and dividends alone, with no return data used
anywhere in the calibration, and is then compared with the returns it
was never shown. Data columns come from the paper (Table I and
Table VII), and the code cell computes the model columns when the page
builds.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
import lrrcs as lrr

solver = lrr.ModelSolver(lrr.get_table_ii_params(), n_x=30, n_s=4).solve()
tab = lrr.simulate_table_vii(solver, n_samples=300, years=74, seed=0)

data_er = {"growth": 7.81, "value": 13.88, "market": 8.56}   # Kiku, Table I
print(f"{'':10s} {'E[R] data':>10s} {'E[R] model':>11s}")
for name in ("growth", "value", "market"):
    print(f"{name:10s} {data_er[name]:10.2f} {tab['mean_return'][name]:11.2f}")
print(f"\nvalue premium: about 6 in the data, "
      f"{tab['value_premium']:.1f} in the model")
print(f"CAPM beta ratio (value/growth): {tab['beta_ratio']:.2f}, "
      f"so value has the lower beta and the higher return")
```

## The course outline

**Part I: The puzzle.** A DCF has
[two free numbers](chapters/01-two-free-numbers.qmd), and fixing them
honestly requires a model of risk. The
[data chapter](chapters/02-value-premium-in-the-data.qmd) documents a
premium of about six percentage points that the CAPM cannot price.

**Part II: The toolkit.**
[The Euler equation](chapters/03-pricing-by-euler-equation.qmd) prices
every claim in the model.
[Epstein-Zin preferences](chapters/04-epstein-zin-preferences.qmd) make
news about future growth affect prices today, and the
[long-run risks consumption process](chapters/05-long-run-risks.qmd)
supplies the news.

**Part III: Solving the model.** The
[log-linear solution](chapters/06-log-linear-solution.qmd) gives closed
form answers, and the
[quadrature solution](chapters/07-quadrature-solution.qmd) avoids the
approximation. Each chapter also explains what its method leaves out.

**Part IV: Testing against the data.** You
[calibrate the cash flows](chapters/08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd)
without using any return data. You then test the model on the
[aggregate market](chapters/09-the-market-test.qmd), and you check
whether the
[value premium comes out right](chapters/10-value-premium-resolved.qmd)
with nothing re-tuned.

**Part V: Applying the model.** You
[price a claim of your own](chapters/11-price-your-own-claim.qmd), and
then you read the
[objections and the model's limits](chapters/12-objections-and-limits.qmd).

If you are new, start with [How to read this course](how-to-read.qmd).
The course does not claim the model is true. The course claims a
valuation should get its forecast and its discount rate from one place,
and the model is a clean working example of how to do so.

::: {.firewall}

prints it at build time, by running the [`lrrcs`](reference/api.qmd)
package on the paper's calibration. Data numbers are the paper's
